utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the case number is: IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President. Just in relation to the next witness, Dean Manning, I don't know how long the examination -- cross-examination will last of the present witness. And Mr. Manning is here, but he's also feeling unwell today. So if you could indicate that we will start with him tomorrow rather than he has to wait until perhaps he will be on late this afternoon, that will be very helpful. But he is here willing and ready to testify today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, will you please tell me how long your cross-examination will last.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I believe we will be able to finish with this witness today. That's the big general answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One session or two sessions. I think we may need to go into the second session. I'm hoping that we won't, but it all depends on, you know, how much interplay we have with the witness here. With respect to Mr. Manning, I understand about his health. I certainly understand, you know, the stress one goes -- undergoes in testifying. I certainly don't want Mr. Manning here if he's not feeling well. I did discuss this matter yesterday with my colleagues on the Prosecution side. And I certainly have no objections to Mr. Manning testifying tomorrow -- starting tomorrow. As for the cross of Mr. Manning, because that's probably your next question I anticipate, I would suspect that it's very, very minimum. We're not talking a session. We're talking literally a very short period of time. So I don't suspect that we're going to need Mr. Manning beyond Friday, assuming that they take a full day on direct, which I'm told, that they will have for Mr. Manning. I've spoken with my colleagues from the Jokic team, and I don't believe that they have that much questioning to do with Mr. Manning. But they would be in a better position to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. We have prepared to examine Mr. Brunborg today. We have four topics or four issues to focus on and ask for explanation or clarification from the witness. We do not believe that this would take longer than 20 minutes. So as far as we're concerned, Mr. Manning can come tomorrow to testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we have decided we will break after the cross-examination and the re-examination of this witness for today. And then tomorrow morning in Courtroom I, we'll hear Mr. Dean Manning. It is so decided. And, Mr. Waespi, do you know or do you happen to know how long your direct examination to Mr. Dean Manning will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It will take the full day, three court sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We have reserved Monday for the whole day for the courtroom, so that if we could not finish Mr. Dean Manning's testimony, we could possibly sit next Monday. Well, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we left off yesterday as we were trying to determine a -- your definition of Srebrenica. And at one point you pointed to a map that was in one of your articles, but which was not located in one of your reports. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge did the Office of the Prosecution or did you ever compile a list of what constituted Srebrenica, and by that I mean aside from the municipality, the settlements that should be included in what we would call Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given a list of all places of disappearance that was relevant for the estimate of the number of missing persons from after the fall of the enclave. Excuse me, may I turn this off, this screen? Okay. Now, it's off. But now I see myself, may I turn myself off? Okay. Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, I do not see really that it is necessary to define Srebrenica as such. We have Srebrenica town, we have the municipality of Srebrenica, and I was asked to estimate the number of people who went missing after the fall of the enclave, defined by the date, after the 11th of July, 1995, and as defined by the places where people were reported as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So from your answer what I get is: As far as you were concerned, given your particular mandate, you didn't think that that was a relevant issue?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defining Srebrenica as such?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew -- I had of course a list of all localities, or naselja as they're called, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So may I --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Srebrenica, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And may I ask: Where did that list come from?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That came from the former Yugoslavia. There was a list and it came from the census and it came from all kinds of statistic publications listing all localities in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I were to ask you then when you come up with this percentage or numerical figure of the estimated persons who are missing from Srebrenica, does that list contain everyone who was within those settlements in addition to the town of Srebrenica, or are you including other places as well. Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm including all of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it -- well, first before we get -- let me ask this question now. I take it that you must have used this particular book. And I'm showing you a book that's titled "National Structure of Settlements, Population of Bosnia and Herzegovina" --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You are familiar?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, I know for a fact that it's in Ewa Tabeau's office, in fact, and so you must have looked at this.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also have my own copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your own copy it would have all the settlements within Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and what have you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's also some other data in this particular book.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so the data, in fact, in this particular book, which incidentally, speaking about this book, just so we all know, and I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can introduce just the title page, Your Honour, for identification purposes, since I am referring to. I'm not -- I don't intend to proffer the entire book, but this would be marked as D111/1 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this particular book basically is a compilation of the statistics generated from the census of 1991, is it not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this was published in Zagreb, which is in Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is, shall we say, a cleaned up version of certain information that was part of the overall census of 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, along with this particular book, there are other volumes which have more specific information, which we will discuss. Are you familiar with the other volumes?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this particular volume we are able to trace, for instance, with respect to the municipality of Srebrenica as an example, all of the settlements that belong or are encompassed within Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There is also a numerical breakdown of the inhabitants of Srebrenica and its settlements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have the number of inhabitants for each place individually. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have an overall number. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have also references to previous years, to prior census data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We also have a numerical breakdown of the number of -- depending on the ethnic background, Croat, Serb, Muslim. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if we were to look at this book that was published in 1995, based on the statistics gathered in the 1991 census, we would be able to see as of 1991 what the general makeup of Srebrenica in each settlement was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So from there we would have a number from which to work with at least?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the other books which contain other information would also contain, for instance, the age groups. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now would agree with me, would you not -- I'll try to speak slower, too. You would agree with me, would you not, that the basis of the census of 1991, as in previous censuses that had taken place in Bosnia -- in the former Yugoslavia, was not to have an accurate listing of all the names of individuals living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was not the primary basis for the census. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was primarily a statistical exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And by statistical exercise, what we're talking about, they were looking primarily for some very certain data such as, first of all, number of overall inhabitants in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Broken down into regions, municipalities, and settlements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They were looking at -- of course we talked about the numerical, plus from that we could derive the percentage of the various ethnic groups living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The number of households?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The number of members of -- in each household?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe there was some other data that might have been relevant or was relevant to the economic status, social status, that sort of stuff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And because that was the primary basis for the census, the actual name of the individual and the personal identification numbers subscribed or given to each person in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not necessarily a vital statistic for this particular census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the names are included because -- to get an idea of the members of each household and for checking purposes. There is often a post-enumeration survey when an enumerator goes back -- a supervisor goes back and checks that they enumerated it correctly. And in that case it's useful to have the names of the household. Also to avoid that, an enumerator picks up the same household twice. It's very useful to have the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Primarily the census was more concerned with the name of the head of the household and not necessarily all of the members of the household?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were more or less on equal status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we now, at least based in part from your own observations, that there were a lot of missing personal identification numbers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are two sets of numbers. The first seven. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from what I'm told, those are the most critical numbers. And then there are six other numbers as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And those numbers were considered personal in nature to such a degree that they were not required to give them?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was -- your -- that's probably correct. Whether they were required or not to tell the enumerators the number, I don't know. I think the census was voluntary. I'm not sure about that, the voluntariness of the census. I'm not sure. I don't know. I don't think it was, actually. There are different laws in different countries about the voluntariness of participating in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So as you were conducting this study, I take it you did not explore -- maybe it was not an issue, and I'm not suggesting that it is an issue, but you did not explore whether this census was a compulsory census, where everybody had to at least give certain information, versus a voluntary census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In most countries it is compulsory. But I did not check their legislation. There was a special census act, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And there was a special law on census in 1991 that was passed also, as I understand?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But if you were to that at least with respect to the personal identification number, providing that particular information was not compulsory, would you take exception with that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may very well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which may also account why there's a fairly large percentage of unaccounted numbers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Now, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identification number did not play an important role in our studies, in our analysis, because for the very reason you are pointing at, it was missing for so many people. We also learned that there were many women, old women, who reported their husband's ID number, for example. So it's not totally reliable, and for that reason we did not rely on it. Moreover, the date of birth, as you mentioned, is included in the "maticni broj," the unique number, but it was also recorded separately. So we could compare those two pieces of information to see how reliable the unique number, the ID number, was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's why you would need both numbers, to make sure that the date of birth that was written in was identical to the seven-digit number. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, would -- given that you had this particular information from the census, do you think this might have been relevant and useful had you been tasked - I think we talked about this yesterday - had you been tasked with coming up with some figures as to the overall impact on the age group in the area of Srebrenica by, for instance, looking at the 1991 census information that we have, the age group, and then perhaps looking at the information that you gathered later on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly looked at that book a lot and the data on the number of people in each locality and the municipality, certainly. The problem was that in July 1995, at the beginning of July, we did not know how many people who remained, of those that were enumerated and recorded in that book, how many people were still in Srebrenica and how many people came from other parts of Bosnia and how many people were killed or migrated out or in. And so ideally we should have had a census on the 1st of July, the 10th of July 1991. Fine that would have been the deal. So we had to deal with the second best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just as a matter of precision, there's no record that I can find, at least in your documents here, that there was any reference or comparisons made to see, you know, what age group was actually determined on the basis of the 1991 census, especially based on an official version versus what you were able to find later on, and perhaps listing why you looked at it but then decided to either disregard it or not give it much weight.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't need it, because I had the whole census, the individual data, so I could calculate my own age distribution. And this is shown in the addendum number 2 of my report -- my addendum report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I take it, if I understand you correctly, because this is an official list, as you well know, versus whatever you looked at, I don't know. You said you looked at the 1991 census and you commented that there were a lot of errors. I believe you used the particular word a "plethora." That was the word. It was kind of interesting. I thought that was quite an exquisite choice of adjectives to use, a plethora of errors that you found. So obviously you would have wanted to look at this version which is the official version, i.e., the cleaned version, to make some comparisons. Would you not agree with me that at least that would have been -- this would have been the more accurate one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because this was published in 1995. The tables were produced in Sarajevo, by people there, and because of the war it was printed in Zagreb. But after 1995, there was -- some corrections were made in the census. There were temporary absent household members and temporary present, and they did the cleaning up of that and some other errors, which formed the basis for the list -- census list that was given to OSCE in connection with the elections. So that may not be and is not necessarily the most correct version of the representation of the census results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Even though it's from the state bureau of statistics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the other volumes that contain other information, did you use the same logic in simply dismissing or not relying on that information, or did you rely on it, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used those other volumes when we needed to. But let me remind you that errors in a spelling of a name has no influence at all in the number of people in a locality or municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or on the age distribution or on the sex distribution because as I said -- recorded separately, neither does an error in the "maticni broj."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, the reason I'm asking all of these questions, because yesterday we talked about certain sources that might have been available to you, such as refugee lists, either in Croatia or Serbia or the RS, Bosnia-Herzegovina, that were at your -- within your grasp and reach and for whatever reason you didn't look at them, at least for no other reason to see for the people who have migrated, where refugees may be, to see whether any of the people on the missing list might be on other lists. So do you recall that conversation we had yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But then I said that I did not manage to get hold of the refugee lists. I learned about them and made several attempts to get the lists but did not succeed at that time. Later my successor, Ewa Tabeau, acquired those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you left -- you left in 19 - what is it - 1998?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You produced a report in 2000. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You testified in the Krstic case in 2000?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You produced in between -- well, you produced an addendum in 2003. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In between 2000 and 2003, you wrote one article in 2001, which we haven't gotten to yet, and one article in 2002. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now as I understand it, you have been assisting or working with an updated version currently being prepared by the demographic team within the OTP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You just indicated that this information came into the hands of your successor, Ewa Tabeau. Would you tell us whether this came into her possession prior to 2000 or after 2000.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, because my task was to look at the number of missing and dead people, not on the number of refugees in this connection. I looked at the number of refugees, displaced persons, in other connections, but not with regard to Srebrenica where I focused on the missing and dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me go back to my question. Yesterday we discussed whether you looked at these other sources of material that was available to see whether you could -- whether that would assist you in having a more reliable, firmer, final analysis of the data that was available to you. Okay. You indicated you didn't know about it. Fair enough. Now you tell us at some point you learned of it. Somebody else, a colleague, is using it. I'm asking you if you know when that information became available; you tell us you don't know. My question is: Should you not have looked at that information, assuming it came in prior to 2000, at least to see whether your analysis was accurate for the preparation of the 2000 report, if for no other reason to see that there are no duplicates. Somebody claims to be living at a refugee while at the same time you have him on the list.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that it did not arrive in 2000, perhaps 2001, as Ewa Tabeau started to work for the Tribunal at the -- in the fall of 2000 as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: So she could not have acquired it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Certainly well before you wrote your addendum to your 2000 report, which was 2003. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if it wasn't available for your 2000 report, the addendum - and as I understand, an addendum is a supplement, an updated version of the previous report, perhaps even including some corrections as a result of new information, new analysis, new methodology, whatever - the addendum should have included that information, if you had thought it was necessary. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, I'm afraid. In this case the addendum highlighted a few special issues. It did not include an updated list of missing persons; that is work in progress. This was the draft material that was given to you on Monday night. And it -- so there is no updated list of missing and dead persons yet, a final list. So in this case my addendum was just highlighting a few pieces of information, additional information, and issues that I knew about -- that I had learned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fair enough to say that the addendum would not have been overburdened, that's what you used yesterday, that term, overburdened by at least making some reference that we have this additional information, we haven't factored it yet, but nonetheless we have this list of refugees which we intend to check and double-check against our list to ensure that the list is continually updated and complete. That could have been included in -- certainly so that somebody like me who would have been interested in double-checking all of this would read it and know, I see, they're doing something about it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, there was no additional list in the addendum, but I'm sure that my -- Ewa Tabeau will consider your proposal, which is an excellent idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, speaking of Ewa Tabeau - I've never met the young lady - I didn't have a chance to read her entire draft carefully and analytically, but I was kind of curious at the very last page, on page 23 -- do you have it by any chance, the draft -- I guess we could -- I need --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could refer to this as D112 for identification purposes. We can put the last page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 23?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, I understand it's merely a draft, but nonetheless drafts are welcomed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure whether Your Honours have this report, because as I stated to the Defence counsel, this was only for disclosure purposes. The Prosecution did not rely on this material. We don't tender it as an exhibit. It was merely disclosure purposes, because that was material which Dr. Brunborg had a look at prior to his testimony. So we felt it was important that the Defence has seen it. But that's why only the Defence has received a copy of this draft but not the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we don't know what's the purpose for the Defence counsel to use this material, but in the cross-examination the party doing the cross could use whatever materials as they could get, so long as the questions are related to the subject matter of this case. But we'll see how Mr. Karnavas presents his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, you're familiar with this draft. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of it, but I haven't studied all of it in detail, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. No need to get defensive already. But on the very first page, it does have your name there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that gave me some confidence this morning as I was reading it that I could probably ask you a few questions about it, since it has your name -- obviously they wouldn't use your name without your permission? Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, now if we look at the very last page, and I understand it's merely a draft, but it goes back to one of my earlier questions. Yesterday I had asked whether there was a definition of Srebrenica. And I pointed in your report, in your first report, where you did not have a definition as far as Srebrenica was concerned, but you did have a definition of terms for Srebrenica victims, which is a little bit different, as you would agree with me. Focusing your attention to page 23 of this draft, which is marked for identification purposes as D112, looking at the second paragraph on page 23, you say -- it says here: "The same logic lies behind the category 'residence: Srebrenica area,' used for all victims whose place of residence in 1991 was in one of the municipalities in the Srebrenica region, but no specific place of disappearance or killing, such as 'at home' et cetera was given in the original source." So here in this particular draft, at least when we're talking about residence and a reference is made to Srebrenica area, we know - or perhaps we don't know, that's the question that we're going to be discussing - that the drafters of this particular report refer to the Srebrenica region, the municipalities in the Srebrenica region. Now, we just concluded discussing -- at least what you told us, that when you prepared your initial list, you relied on the official list of the settlements within the Srebrenica municipality, and you did the same thing for Vlasenica, for Bratunac, et cetera, et cetera. In this draft we're talking about a Srebrenica region, and perhaps you can assist us here. What is meant and what are the geographical boundaries by Srebrenica region? Because officially, at least in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, I believe, is a technical term used in this appendix or this draft report, and it refers to as one of the municipalities in Srebrenica region, including the municipality of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Zepa, and I think Han Pijesak. I'm not quite sure. But here it's probably listed earlier in the draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you could find it. I mean, I -- but --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are the opstinas of disappearance, but these are opstinas of disappearance, not of residence. Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Rogatica Vlasenica, Kalesija, Kladanj, Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this was some additional information that was obtained, this opstina of disappearance?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you know the place of disappearance, then -- and you know where the place is, then you automatically have the municipality of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But work with me here for a second, and this is not a trick question, this is for the record that we all need to know. When you say here that the municipalities in the Srebrenica region used for all victims whose place of residence was in one of the municipalities in the Srebrenica region, is it your understanding that when we're talking about residence, Srebrenica area, we are talking about all of these places, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Rogatica, Vlasenica - and then you go - Bijeljina, is that all within what you would consider the Srebrenica region for the purposes of identifying residence of the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I please, it is -- this is work in progress, it was a draft. And I was not prepared -- I'm not prepared to discuss this. I don't -- haven't even read the last page. Because it got to me very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if you will excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will. But if I could just ask you one question. I'm not trying to embarrass you or try to put you on the spot. But would you not agree with us that that definition is a rather inconsistent definition, given what we find in the official statistics book, you know, from the bureau of statistics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a completely different purpose. That is an municipal -- a municipality is a municipal area. It has an elected council and everything. It has localities, or naselja. Now we talked about -- when you talk about where people lived before the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica, where they disappeared, that is a completely different issue. If you look at Table 1 in my addendum, you will see where the missing men came from. They came from Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Han Pijesak, and other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we know this because we matched the missing men with their residence in 1991. So this is a pragmatic definition. It's not [indiscernible], logical, geographical or anything. But obviously these municipalities are not far from Srebrenica. So -- and why do they come from other municipalities than Srebrenica? Because they took refuge for some reason or not in the municipality of Srebrenica or the town before 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first you would agree with me that trying to identify the places of where these people came from, you know, these missing persons as opposed to a region might be an important question for us to determine here in court?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before I get to how you arrived at your numbers, do you know whether there was a difference in stating the place of residence when the census was done versus when the information was collected by the ICRC or the PHR?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they did not ask about place of residence, did they? I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what about place of birth?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Place of birth is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And of course place of birth is not the same as place of residence. People may have moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the 1991 census, do you know how people listed their place of birth versus how it was --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did they ask for place of birth or municipality or birth? I think they asked for place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that in that part of the world that when the census was done the place of birth, a mother would put down or would be put down where of -- the place of the mother's permanent residence?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what is usually done. It's done in Norway, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So even if, say, the child is born in Belgrade in a hospital, they would put down if they were from Bratunac, Bratunac as opposed to Belgrade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is according to vital statistic principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But if you were to ask folks in that region that question, you were to ask a mother, she would give you not her place of birth, but rather the actual place where the birth took place, in other words they would say Belgrade and not Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you think that information might skew some of your statistics that you relied on from the 1991 census when we're trying to define where the people's residency was or where they came from?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. Because, as I said, we obtained the place of residence through matching census data and missing persons data. So it -- we were not really very much concerned about place of birth. Moreover, we looked at place of birth in difficult cases to see that the place of birth was not really very far away -- or no, the place of residence was not far away. But place of birth did not play a significant role. And moreover, usually a place of birth is in a nearby hospital, a hospital not very far from the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, the statistics that you have, as I understand it and we're just going to go over this very briefly again, when you were compiling the list, the initial list, when you went through the ICRC list and the PHR list, at some point -- well, the first go around you had -- there was some perfect matches or some matches. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell us the percentage of that. Was it -- how many were actually a 100 per cent perfect match, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, but we have that in our log.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it a high percentage or a low percentage?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm it's for your perspective, anything over -- was it over above 50 or below 50?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was below 50. Somewhere between 20 and 40 probably. .

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and then you indicated the next step that you took was to widen -- to take a wider approach?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the example that you gave was to use the first initial, last name. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then -- and I believe you indicated that the reason you did that was because you wanted to be on the conservative side?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that if we found a match that was then equally last name and first initial, it was not accepted as such unless other information also was consistent. So if the name was first name, the initial was the same, then it was spelling, two letters were interchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there's no need to try to get ahead of my cross-examination. I understand.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know your line of examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Good. If you just listen to my questions, we're going to get along fine. And I -- whenever you need to explain, explain away. Okay. Now, why didn't you, for instance, use another approach, if I may suggest one, at least if not this time, for the next time, why not say, okay, after you had all these perfect matches, then go back and, for instance, try to widen the spectrum by first choosing the first three or four letters of the name, plus last name, run it up to the computer to see how many come up, either for Bosnia-Herzegovina or for Eastern Bosnia. Then -- so you probably would come up with a certain number. Then widen the search a little bit more by first initial, last name, you probably would come up with a much larger number, of course. And then finally, first initial, first name, first initial, last name. And then you would have a much wider range. And then you can begin a process of elimination now that you have looked at basically the universe of choices available to you. And of course the first thing that you would do is shorten it to the particular area, which would be Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, whatever -- however you wanted to do it. Would that not -- taking that approach, would you not say that though it's much more cumbersome, much more time-consuming, much more labour-intensive, would you not say that through that approach you would have a much more, for lack of a better term, reliable outcome, rather than your approach where a certain amount of fuzziness, if I may borrow your term, needed to be used in order to correct some of the errors or omissions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fail to see that that would be the case. Fuzziness is not my term; it's used in statistics and mathematics. And the results would have been the same, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- okay. If I may -- and I didn't mean to interrupt you, but if I could get a word in, although you're probably saying when are you going to get a word in. Right? In doing that process you would have been able to also mark down and keep track of the percentages, the number of people you came up with and the percentage, so at each stage we would have, for instance, all of this data. And then when you arrive at the last figure, we would be able to look at that figure and you would be able to reason exactly how you got to that figure, as opposed to what you did, and I'm not necessarily saying that it was an incorrect process, but I would say perhaps you took some shortcuts, that because of the limited nature of the pool that you were looking at, a certain degree of fuzziness, subjectivity, was required in order to make the matches occur?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that we could have followed your approach. The end results would have been exactly the same. If you -- whether you do all the exact matches first and then mark them, and actually you don't have to consider them anymore, or do it the other way around, it shouldn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You would agree with me that my approach is a much more comprehensive approach?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comprehensive, yes, perhaps. I don't really see much difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When I ask you now, can you tell me: When you came up with that general figure of the matches, of 5.000 I believe or 6.000 between -- I think it was 5.000 between PHR list and the ICRC list, was that a perfect, perfect match, or was that a match with some fuzziness?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used fuzzy criteria to find potential matches, and then we checked whether this fuzziness could be explained. We wouldn't accept any fuzziness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But how much fuzziness, if we could give a percentage, ultimately was used? 10 per cent? 20 per cent? 30 per cent?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to tell. But at every -- any stage we counted the number of new matches. So whether -- let me give an example. If the year of birth was 1951 in one case and 1950 in the other case, we would accept that if everything else was the same or almost the same, identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if the father's name, if available, was different, then of course we would not accept 1950/1951 as a correct match.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, then after you made this comparison, then you were able to come to a percentage of 87 per cent, I believe, between the ICRC -- or the master list and the voting -- the census list of 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 87 per cent of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say that was 87 per cent?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: 87 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's assuming, that's assuming, that the information, both from the master list and the 1991 list, is accurate?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's -- assume that they are accurate or almost accurate or are similar. As I said before, names are misspelled, like LJ was sometimes interpreted as Q. So we checked such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The assumption must be made, however, that these are -- this is accurate data in order, you know -- plus or minus something, you know, some error, but accurate data in order for you to come up with this 87 per cent. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That 87 per cent was based on the number of not matches where we were very certain that we were -- that the records from each source were representing the same person, because the names were absolutely identical or almost identical, year of birth was exactly, date of birth exactly the same or almost the same. And every other items were similar and so on. So there would be very little doubt that these were correct matches. On the other hand, we excluded a number of cases where we suspected that these two records probably represent the same person, but we cannot be sure. So to be on the safe side, let's drop them into the box of the 13 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But the 87 per cent -- I guess I'm trying to really get a handle on this, are these all perfect matches, or do they include some guesstimation on your part?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it guesstimation. That is much to lose. It is concerned -- it's based on hard principles and a lot of exact matches, a lot of information -- exact information, but with some adjustment mainly because of errors in the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And could you give me a percentage, could you give me a percentage of how many -- what's the percentage from the 87 per cent that are not exact?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We have included -- we can look at our log.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then based on that 87 per cent you did a breakdown?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And determined, you know, based on the information that you had, what was from Srebrenica, who was from Vlasenica, and what have you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you looked at that information, were you referring to the settlements from this official log or something similar, or was it the general Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we referred to the municipality, the number which was given in the census for each person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if it said Srebrenica, they went in the Srebrenica box?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then after that is when you did some further adjustments, correct, because you had that 13 per cent that didn't match?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so for the 13 per cent, as I understand it, you used --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We prorated, if I may tell you the word you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was looking for the right term. Okay. You prorate it, and then you came up and said, okay, from this 13 per cent we can add X amount to Srebrenica, X amount to Vlasenica, and so on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you felt that that was a comfortable way of doing it because in your mind, and as I understand it's perfectly okay, when you have a fairly large number, such as 87 per cent, assuming that's correct - an assumption I'm not willing to take - but assuming it's correct, then you can go ahead and prorate and to -- with a certain degree of exactitude be right on the money? Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's standard procedure. All right. And that's how you came up with the overall figure.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say that the 56 per cent of people who lived in Srebrenica of those missing persons is the same whether you look at 87 per cent or little -- 100 per cent. It was 56 per cent. Of those 87 per cent, we matched. When we prorate we still get 56 per cent. Because we just distribute equally. It does not affect the proportion who came from different municipalities at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But of course, of the 40.000 -- or the number of people who were there living in Srebrenica, we don't know first the exact number. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And certainly you're not prepared to state that of all the people that were living in that area, many of whom were, you know, left through the woods, the exodus, some died, others were transferred to Tuzla, okay, you're not prepared to say that that 56 per cent also represents the whole of that community, whoever was living in Srebrenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It's -- as you know, almost all these people were men, so it is probably not a bad estimate of the distribution of the men in Srebrenica before -- in July 1995, before the fall. But we can't be sure, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- okay. If I could have one moment. Now, I want to switch to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I would prefer at this point to take a short break, Your Honour, only because I'm having some problems with my one foot. And I promise to be rather efficient in the next session. And I don't think I will need the -- you know, more than half an hour or 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's almost time for the break. Let's resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I thought we could sort of wrap up the issue of sources and data with some final questions here. Now, if I look at your article that you published in 2001, which is called Contribution of Statistical Analysis for the Investigations of the International Tribunal, dated 18, 2000 -- it doesn't have a date. 18, 2001. And for identification purposes, it will be D113. Do you have it handy there by any chance?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have got it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You did author this article, did you not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it says here that it was with the permission -- with permission from IOS Press, Amsterdam, the Netherlands. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: IOS, that is the publisher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it, as in the article we talked about yesterday, that is dated 2002, July 10, which was marked for identification purposes as D110, you sought permission from ICTY to write about this or --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it they looked at it, perhaps might have even commented on it. But in any event you got the green light to go ahead and have it published. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could direct your attention to page 228, and it has an ERN number of 01121254. You will find the number of the page on the left-hand -- upper left-hand. Okay. If we could look at just very briefly the last paragraph before you get into section 2. You state here: "Lack of data is the most serious problem when estimating the number of victims in a war, especially the number of deaths. Identifying and acquiring such data are important tasks. Moreover, the quality of the data, when available, varies tremendously and much time has to be spent checking and revising the data." Now, do you recall writing that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that's your position?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was well said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I also note, if we could go to page 232, with the ER number of 01121258 you state here, right after subsection C where it talks about genocide, you state: "Thus, it is an important task for a demographer to identify, acquire, validate and improve relevant data. Much time has to be spent contacting national and international governmental and nongovernmental institutions and organisations." And I take it that you still maintain that that is a correct approach?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Yet -- now, if I could -- we did discuss that there were some perhaps omissions -- and I'm not saying intentional, but there were some omissions on your part to look at or collect or analyse certain data or sources. We talked about it yesterday; we talked about it briefly earlier. But now, if I could focus your attention to your report dated 12 February, 2000, which has been marked for identification purposes as P725. And if we could look at page 2, sort of the second paragraph, you state here: "Several organisations collected data on persons missing after the fall of Srebrenica, including the International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC, and Physicians for Human Rights, PHR." My question at this point in time, in light of what you previously stated in your articles, that you need to identify and acquire all of the data: Could you please tell us, what are those several other organisations that collected data on persons missing after the fall of Srebrenica that you are aware of, or were aware of.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of one organisation called Muslims Against Genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, that organisation -- some of the data from that organisation is being incorporated into the draft report that we just looked at that is being authored by a host of people, including Ewa Tabeau and yourself as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe -- I don't recall the identification number on this one, but I believe it was D112. We're not going to go into that, but were you aware of that organisation at the time that you compiled your -- you did your 2000 report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I became aware of that organisation at the end of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please give us an explanation as to why there is no reference to that organisation or why you do not use any of the data in that organisation -- from that organisation, yet it would appear from glancing at the draft, 2004 draft, that your successor has to some extent looked into their data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I became aware of it, that organisation had focused mainly on Sarajevo and not on much work on Srebrenica yet. That was the main reason why I did not use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, at some point they did begin to focus on Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was prior to 2003. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yet, in your addendum, again there is no reference that there is this additional data that is being collected, albeit by an NGO, a local NGO, but there's no reference in your report anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I mentioned in the previous session, my addendum did not include an updated list. That is work in progress. I just wanted to highlight a few special aspects that would come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I take it when you prepared your addendum, not only you made no references to it, but you failed in any way to incorporate that information or to perhaps even ask the OTP to look into it to see how that might influence either in a positive or a negative fashion your previous report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed with OTP how it could be used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the addendum, as I understand it given the date of it, it would appear that it was made in preparation for your testimony here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because initially you were on the master list of witnesses for the Prosecution, and we are grateful that you are here testifying. So it would appear that you knew or should have known that you would have been questioned regarding all of the available data related to Srebrenica, the victims of Srebrenica, and so on and so forth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yet when you prepared this addendum, you failed, as we have indicated, to mention this additional data, but also to factor it in. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because it was work in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, where in it -- where in this report pray tell does it note that there is -- there is this data available by this organisation that is being considered by OTP through their demographic team, the results of which are unavailable at that time. Is there any place in your addendum where you make reference to that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is not, because I didn't consider it my responsibility to point out all possible data sources in that addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yesterday, sir - and correct me if I'm wrong - you told us that you were a data junkie --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said data freak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or data freak. Okay. Well, I think either one I'll accept. All right. And I hope that you don't take it in the wrong way but --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Junkies are addicted, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was going to mention the distinction, but thank you for pointing that out. And it is a major distinction. So -- but nonetheless, you would agree with me that given your description, a data freak would be one that in many ways who is sensitive to and enjoys looking at data. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Much the same fashion, as I indicated, I have with footnotes. Now, given your predilection for data, don't you think it would have been helpful for us or for anyone reading your report, for you to have listed the organisations that were collecting data on persons missing after the fall of Srebrenica. So at least if you were not interested in that data, in spite of your -- you being a data freak, others might want to look at that data, at least for the sake of seeing whether there is something there that might in any way either support or take away from some of the conclusions that you have reached in your reports.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my successor, Ewa Tabeau, has mentioned my -- and other related sources in a number of articles and expert reports. But as I said, I did not consider it my task to mention all the possible data sources in that addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, believe it or not, what I'm referring to is the first report of 12 February, 2002. This is where you say: "Several organisations collected data." It's on page 2.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was 2000 -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 2000, 2000, report. Okay. Second page, you know, first paragraph from the top where you say: "Several organisations collected." Can you list the several organisations outside the two that you have listed, and outside the one that you have already told us. Because you said "several." So are you aware of only these three, or are there more? And if so, who are they?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were -- what do you call? It's an institute of war crimes, something -- I don't remember -- recall the exact name in Sarajevo headed by Professor Cekic [phoen], something. There was also the now defunct -- another organisation collecting data on war crimes and victims. There are the women of Srebrenica, the mothers of Srebrenica, who else? Probably several others, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And given -- I take it, I take it, if you were to go back to your notes or your files, somewhere we would be able to find this master list of organisations that you were aware of at the time that you were collecting this data, analysing it, processing, writing reports. Somewhere you must have the list, correct, or is it just from the top of your head hearing anecdotally that there are organisations collecting data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not anecdotally. I heard about organisations. I inquired about what kind of data did they have. Would they make it -- the data accessible to us? What was it worth getting? Was it different from what we had already. So I made several contacts. Some were futile; they led to nothing. I asked again and again. The now defunct organisation which I don't remember the name of was visiting three or four times with no success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I abstract -- make a summary of my travel reports from the missions to Bosnia, I could list all the organisations that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Needless to say, we don't have that listing in your report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And needless to say, we don't have any explanations as to why you chose to totally disregard this data. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when I wrote this report, those were the only data available; that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wait a second. Hold it, hold it. Are you saying that the only data available was the ICRC and the PHR? Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a rudimentary [indiscernible] data were also available. Because as I said these Muslims -- again, genocide had just started on Sarajevo, but not completed. So I did not find it worthwhile to use the -- their data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, let me go back to what you stated and let me remind you that you have a Ph.D. from one of the finest universities in America, now the University of Michigan, where English is spoken. So I assume that you're extremely careful and precise when you use, you know, the Queen's language. And you state: "Several organisations collected data on persons missing after the fall of Srebrenica, including ..." So from this, when I read it, I can conclude that organisations are out there collecting data. Okay. So aside from the three, you were aware of at that time when you were writing this report in 2000 that there was this data out there being collected specifically concerning the events of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically. I did not focus specifically on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me rephrase it. Some of which was specifically related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, certainly you've told us about one organisation, the name of which you don't know, that is currently defunct and was uncooperative or perhaps their data was not particularly enlightening. But other organisations, such as the one with respect to the Srebrenica mothers, surely you're not suggesting that they would not have been interested in providing you with the information that they had, such as the name of their loved ones, place of birth, where they were last seen, all of that. Surely that information could have been gathered from you and your team. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with them and asked to have lists, comprehensive lists of victims or missing persons. While they said they had some, but they did not have any comprehensive lists, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless there you were trying to put these lists together, trying to come up with a master list --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not trying to get a master list of organisations; I was trying to get a master list of missing and dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. And perhaps these other organisations might have been able to provide you with data that you could have incorporated into your study. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps and some has been acquired later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I want to remind you where you indicate that: "Identifying and acquiring such data are important tasks. Moreover, the quality of the data, when available," and you go on, "varies tremendously as much time -- and much time has to be spent checking and revising the data." This is from your article that I just read, which is marked for identification as D111. Now, could it be, sir, that -- or D113, I'm sorry. Could it be that perhaps you didn't have the time or the inclination to spend looking at that data and incorporating that data, that that's why you chose to disregard it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resources and time were certainly an aspect, but it was also quality aspect, that evaluating those data sources, the ICRC and the Physicians for Human Rights missing data lists, taught me that these are very promising -- very comprehensive large data files of good quality. And I was also acquiring and evaluating and assessing the census data and lists of voters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also worked many other areas in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Say that again.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Srebrenica was not the only focus of my work. I said other responsibilities also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I thought I was very careful yesterday to try to elicit your mandate. And we began by stating the first, you were seconded for approximately six months, and your general task was to look for missing people or to compile a list of missing people for the whole country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But then at some point your mission was narrowed by the Office of the Prosecution, because after all it was only you and one assistant initially. And your mandate was to focus, to focus, on Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I specify?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: My original mandate was to look at the population movements, so demographic effects of the conflict in Bosnia, including both missing persons, deaths, refugees, displaced persons, ethnic cleansing. It was a very wide mandate. Now, after a while -- and I was -- did not have an assistant at the beginning; I was alone. This was a, I would say a -- not a trial, not in the legal sense, but it was an experiment, because this was the first time a demographer was employed at the War Crimes Tribunal, so they wanted to see what can we get out of this. And then over the next year or so, one project was singled out as being very interesting and important, and that was Srebrenica. But I also worked on other projects like Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I certainly hope that this has not been an experiment of an endeavour on your part, that is, this work regarding Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you said "experiment," that was your term. Because, if I may add, if I may add, this is not the first time that atrocities ever occurred someplace, okay, and demography has been used elsewhere, for instance, as you mentioned yesterday, with what happened to the Jewish people in, you know, during World War II, what the Turks did to the Armenians, what's going on in Chechnya, East Timor, Cambodia, I can go down the list. So demography has been used in one way or another, along with statisticians, to show the trauma or atrocities has on populations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And there are other reasons that have been used, such as where, you know, ecological reasons, where natives, you know, have been affected as well because of the change of the environment. Correct? So the use of demography in this field is not something unique.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that it was the first time the -- that the ICTY had a demographer, a professional demographer, a population statistician on its staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a trial, it was not a permanent position; it was an ad hoc position for a year. And it resulted in a permanent position and a staff of -- which at the most was -- consisted of five or six people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- now, you said one of your tasks initially was to assess the effects on the population. I believe that was one of the terms you used.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So I would suspect that with regard to Srebrenica, that would have been something that you must have been interested in, the effects on the community of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we've indicated in your report, your two reports, other than statistics, we don't have much, other than certain percentages. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I believe I asked, perhaps I did not, whether it would have been useful for you to have looked at the -- compared the 1991 census list with the voter registration list to look at the age structure so we could have some sort of an indicator. I believe I asked that. Did I ask that question?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so. I don't remember my answer, but I don't think that would be very useful, because the voter list consists only of people over the age of 18. And it's just a sample of the population because everybody did not register to vote. So it doesn't tell us a lot about the age structure of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But in light of the fact that it is a voluntary basis that people register to vote and we have this census, okay, that means if we did the comparison to look at -- or to make a demographic impact assessment study, the figures would be on the conservative side, because it wouldn't -- by your own omission, not everybody who was qualified to vote might have registered. Correct? But nonetheless, we would have at least a certain demographical impact assessment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at that. And it -- originally I thought when I acquired the pre-war census and the post-war source, as the voters' register, I thought, wow, this is great. Now we have the population before the conflict and after the conflict. The difference is victims, consists of victims. But the proportion of those who registered to vote was too low for that. It varied between, say, 60, 70, 80 per cent. And there were many -- those 10 to 30 per cent who did not register, very few of them were killed or were victims. Most of them did not register because they did not feel like for some reason or not, or they were not able to, but not because they were killed.
